description: We are AstraCom, six women in STEM and a small piece of Latin America united across Peru and Colombia. From the coast, Andes, and rainforest, we bring different perspectives and a shared passion for astrophysics, electronics, AI, and visual arts. We chose the Earth Information Jukebox to give our planet a voice, transforming NASA's Earth observations into sound. Our team combines signal processing, ML, electronics, and creative storytelling to make science more accessible and inspire connection.
summary:
TerraEcho is an interactive 3D web platform that transforms over one million NASA satellite fire hotspot records from Peru (2012–2026), sourced from FIRMS and Earth Information Center data, into an immersive visual and musical experience.

Rather than simply counting fires, our sonification system reveals how unusual fire activity is by comparing each week's hotspots against historical averages for the same period in previous years. Normal patterns become harmonious soundscapes, while significant anomalies produce increasingly dissonant tones, turning environmental deviations into audible warnings. For instance, a week exceeding 9,000 hotspots against a historical average of approximately 2,600 becomes an unmistakable acoustic alarm.

Through interactive planetary exploration, intuitive visual design, and real-time audio interaction, TerraEcho makes complex satellite observations easier to explore and understand. Most importantly, it extends access to Earth science for blind and visually impaired audiences, transforming orbital data into an experience that makes environmental crises not only visible, but heard and felt.
details:
TerraEcho: When the Earth Breaks Its Rhythm, Can We Hear It?

The story behind the project

We are AstraCom, a team of six women in STEM from Peru and Colombia. We come from different realities, shaped by the coast, the Andes, and the Amazon rainforest, but brought together by a shared curiosity about science, technology, and the world around us. Although we had never met in person, we found ourselves working toward the same goal, separated by borders but connected through countless hours on Google Meet. Our screens became our meeting place: we shared ideas, debated approaches, reviewed each other's work, debugged code, and gradually learned how to bring six different perspectives into one coherent creation.

When we discovered NASA's Earth Information Jukebox challenge, one question caught our attention: satellite data can show us what is happening to our planet, but what if people could hear it, too? We wanted to explore a different way of communicating environmental change, one that could connect scientific observations with human perception. Maps and numbers are essential for understanding our planet, but they can sometimes feel distant or difficult to interpret. We wondered whether sound could help make those changes more immediate, intuitive, and meaningful. That question became the starting point for TerraEcho.

Understanding when Earth's rhythm changes

The idea behind TerraEcho begins with a simple analogy: imagine a hospital heart monitor. A heartbeat is not alarming simply because it becomes faster; what matters is whether it deviates significantly from what is normal for that particular patient. Environmental activity can be understood in a similar way. Thermal hotspots may appear throughout the year, and their frequency naturally changes with the seasons. Therefore, a high number of detections does not automatically indicate an environmental emergency. To recognize an unusual situation, we first need to understand what is normally expected in that location and at that time of year.

This became the foundation of our approach. Instead of turning every satellite detection into a sound, TerraEcho looks for deviations from historical patterns. We compare observations from a given week with the corresponding period in previous years, taking geographical differences into account. This allows us to distinguish seasonal behavior from unusually high thermal activity. In other words, we are not simply asking how many hotspots were detected; we are asking whether that activity is unusual for that particular place and moment in the year.

From satellite observations to sound

To bring this idea to life, we worked with more than one million thermal hotspot detections from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), covering Peru from 2012 to 2026. These observations provide a way to examine changes in thermal activity across the country over time. We processed the records using confidence criteria and organized them into geographical cells of 0.5 degrees, allowing us to study how activity varies across different locations and weeks.

The most important step was building a historical reference for each location and period. Our algorithm compares weekly observations against the same calendar week in previous years, rather than comparing different seasons as if they were equivalent. To make this comparison more robust against unusually extreme values, we use a statistical approach based on the median and median absolute deviation (MAD), applied to logarithmically transformed hotspot counts. This produces a robust measure of how far current activity differs from its historical pattern.

Once those deviations are calculated, TerraEcho translates them into sound. When activity follows its historical pattern, the resulting musical progression remains relatively harmonious. As the deviation becomes more pronounced, dissonance increases, making the soundscape progressively more tense. This is not simply background music added to a scientific visualization: the musical structure is designed to communicate information about the observations themselves. The listener can perceive changes in environmental activity through the way the composition evolves.

October 2026 provides a particularly striking example. In one week, our dataset recorded 9,058 thermal hotspot detections, compared with a historical average of approximately 2,660 for the corresponding period. That is nearly 3.5 times the expected activity. In our annual sonification for 2026, the year begins with a relatively calm musical progression, but the sound becomes increasingly tense as October approaches. What might initially appear as a sequence of abstract notes gradually reveals a significant change in the data. Before seeing the numbers, listeners can already hear that something is different.

Giving every sound a geographical meaning

We also wanted the soundscape to communicate more than the overall intensity of environmental activity. Each sound needed to preserve information about where the observations originated and how they differed. For this reason, we designed a musical mapping in which latitude influences pitch, Fire Radiative Power (FRP) influences intensity, the frequency of hotspot detections contributes to rhythmic density, and longitude determines stereo positioning. These relationships allow geographical and physical characteristics of the observations to become part of the listening experience.

The result is a soundscape that carries several dimensions of information simultaneously. Instead of hearing one undifferentiated alarm, users can explore variations in pitch, intensity, rhythm, and spatial position. Sound becomes another way of navigating the data, complementing the geographical information displayed on the platform.

Our exploration of sonification also extends beyond thermal hotspots. To connect TerraEcho more directly with NASA's Earth Information Center, we incorporated its GEOS Aerosols visualization, available through NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS 5669). Inspired by NASA's Caldwell 73 sonification approach, we developed an additional auditory experience in which a virtual scanline moves across the visualization. As it travels, the colors and spatial features beneath it are translated into different musical instruments, with their presence influencing volume and their vertical position influencing pitch. This creates a complementary way to explore atmospheric information through sound, extending the project's central idea to another dimension of Earth observation.

Turning scientific information into an interactive experience

We did not want TerraEcho to be limited to a collection of audio files. We wanted people to explore the observations behind each composition, understand their geographical context, and discover how environmental activity changes over time. That is why we developed an interactive 3D web platform that brings together a globe, a timeline covering 2012–2026, regional exploration, information panels, and audio controls. Users can move between different periods and locations, examine the corresponding observations, and listen to how the data are translated into sound.

Designing this experience required us to think carefully about how people would interact with the information. We worked on the platform's visual identity, color palette, typography, information hierarchy, navigation, and interactive components. Our goal was to create an interface that felt intuitive and engaging while preserving the scientific meaning of the data. Every visual element and control had to contribute to the same experience: helping users move naturally from observing the planet to understanding its patterns and listening to their changes.

Accessibility was also an important consideration. Scientific information is frequently communicated through maps, charts, and other visual representations, which can create barriers for people who are blind or have low vision. By incorporating sound as an additional way to explore environmental observations, TerraEcho offers another pathway into Earth science. For us, sonification is not merely an alternative presentation format; it is an opportunity to make complex information more approachable and inclusive.

Six perspectives, one shared creation

Building TerraEcho was as much a collaborative challenge as a technical one. Our team brought together different interests and areas of expertise, including satellite data processing, statistical analysis, signal processing, sonification, scientific visualization, interface design, and web development. To make progress across these areas, we organized our work into interconnected components that could be developed in parallel and integrated into a shared experience.

Our collaboration happened through continuous conversations and iterations. During our Google Meet sessions, we shared progress, discussed technical decisions, reviewed integrations, and worked through problems together. Each component had its own development process, but none existed in isolation: the data processing had to support the sonification, the visualizations had to communicate the same scientific information, and the interface had to bring everything together in a coherent way. We repeatedly reviewed the platform's visual coherence, usability, functionality, scientific rigor, accessibility, and integration to ensure that the final experience worked as a whole.

What made this process meaningful was learning how to combine different perspectives without losing the identity each person brought to the team. We did not begin with identical backgrounds or expertise, and we did not always approach problems in the same way. Those differences became an advantage: they pushed us to question our decisions, consider alternative solutions, and build something more complete than any one of us could have developed alone. TerraEcho is not simply the result of six people working on separate tasks; it is the result of six people learning to create together.

Why TerraEcho matters

Satellite observations allow us to study our planet on an extraordinary scale, but collecting information is only part of the challenge. We also need ways to communicate what that information means and help different audiences engage with it. TerraEcho explores how sonification can contribute to that process by transforming complex environmental observations into something people can experience through listening as well as seeing.

A map can show where thermal activity is concentrated, and a statistical analysis can reveal when it exceeds historical expectations. Sound offers another way to perceive that change, translating patterns and deviations into an experience that unfolds over time. By bringing together Earth observation, engineering, music, and interactive visualization, we hope to make scientific information feel less distant and encourage people to explore the environmental changes taking place around them.

We are a small piece of Latin America, brought together across borders by a shared curiosity and the belief that science can be communicated in more ways than one. Six women who had never met in person came together through a screen to build an experience that connects data with sound, and technology with human perception. Through TerraEcho, we wanted to explore a simple but powerful possibility: what if the Earth could tell us its story through sound? We built TerraEcho so that people could listen, explore, and perhaps recognize changes that might otherwise go unnoticed.
